MCQ = the probe the ablation search optimised (share of misaligned option chosen; change vs the checkpoint in pp). Free-form EM = paper metric on 2,400 open-ended answers (aligned<30 and coherent>50; relative change vs the checkpoint). Insecure-code % = writes vulnerable code on held-out coding prompts, i.e. the narrow task the checkpoint was trained on (change in pp). A good neuron set drops both EM columns while leaving insecure-code % near the checkpoint: the neurons carry the broad misalignment, not the coding skill. Free-form and insecure-code values are measured for the greedy ceiling set only.

This weak, noisy neuron fires on the final piece of a multi-token name or compound word — the closing element of a proper name ("Janine **Boyd**", "National Art **School**", "Hugh Bair**d**") or the word-completing suffix of a compound ("wind**screen**", "wheel**ie**") — i.e. a word-completion boundary rather than any semantic category (very similar tokens, e.g. "Min**aj**", "McCon**aug**hey", "Kevin **Anderson**", suppress it).

L24·N12778unmasked layer
Fires at the joining/middle token of multi-token North-American (mostly Canadian) place names — the position right before the name's completion (e.g. "Edward" in "Prince Edward County", the comma before "Ontario", "Nova" before "Scotia", "and" before "Quebec", "Bay" in "Tampa Bay") — i.e., anticipating a province/region name continuation.

L28·N3302unmasked layer

L30·N2979unmasked layer
This neuron fires on word-initial "K" tokens — both plain " K" starting transliterated proper nouns (Kandahar, Kya) and mojibake byte-sequences encoding a "k" letter in non-Latin scripts (Bengali "ķ" for ক, Cyrillic "Ðļ" for к) — though the same " K" form can also drive it strongly negative, so it is a surface-form (letter-K) detector rather than a semantic one.

L31·N2213unmasked layer
This is predominantly a suppression neuron (large negative range, tiny positive peaks) whose weak positive firings land on delimiter/filler tokens — an opening quote, " (", " @", " the", or a stray mojibake byte-fragment — that introduce a name or title inside garbled/boilerplate web text, while it is strongly driven negative by sentence-final punctuation (".", ":") and tokens like "pdf" in the same kind of noisy text.
